space.text: The solar system has one star, eight planets, five officially named dwarf planets, and thousands of comets and asteroids.
The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a dense cloud of gas and dust.
Our solar system is in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.
The Sun contains more than 99 percent of the matter that was available in the early solar system.
Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are rocky terrestrial planets.
Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
The asteroid belt is made of leftover pieces of the early solar system that did not form a planet.
The Kuiper Belt is a ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune's orbit.
Pluto is smaller than Earth's Moon and has five known moons.
The Oort Cloud is a predicted spherical shell around the solar system; it has not been directly observed.
Voyager 1 crossed the heliosphere into interstellar space in 2012.
Voyager 2 crossed the heliosphere into interstellar space in 2018.
The solar system orbits the center of the Milky Way once about every 230 million years.
Earth's average distance from the Sun defines one astronomical unit, or AU.
The four outer giant planets have rings, although Saturn's are the most prominent from Earth.
Jupiter takes about 9.9 hours to rotate once, the shortest planetary day in our solar system.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm that has lasted for hundreds of years.
Venus is the hottest planet in our solar system.
A rotation on Venus takes longer than one trip around the Sun: about 243 Earth days versus 225.
Mercury and Venus are the only planets with no moons.
The Sun's visible surface is called the photosphere.
The Sun is a star at the center of our solar system.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
The solar wind is a stream of electrically charged particles flowing outward from the Sun.
The heliosphere is a bubble formed by the solar wind around the solar system.
A comet's tail points away from the Sun because of sunlight and the solar wind.
Most asteroids orbit the Sun in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
The four inner planets have solid, rocky surfaces.
The solar system includes hundreds of moons orbiting planets, dwarf planets, and asteroids.
The Milky Way's Sun sits in a small section called the Orion Arm, or Orion Spur.

moon.text: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite.
The Moon is about 384,400 kilometers from Earth on average.
The Moon is tidally locked, so the same hemisphere always faces Earth.
The Moon rotates once in about the same time it takes to orbit Earth: 27 Earth days.
From Earth, the Moon appears to orbit us about every 29 days because Earth is moving too.
Moon phases happen as we see changing portions of its sunlit half.
A full moon happens when the Moon's Earth-facing hemisphere is fully lit by the Sun.
A new moon occurs when the side facing Earth is dark and the far side is sunlit.
The Moon has a very thin atmosphere called an exosphere.
The Moon has no rings and no moons of its own.
The Moon's surface is rocky and marked by impact craters.
The Moon's gravity at its surface is about one-sixth of Earth's gravity.
Apollo astronauts brought 382 kilograms of lunar rocks and soil back to Earth.
More than 105 robotic spacecraft have been launched to explore the Moon.
A Soviet spacecraft first flew past the Moon's far side in 1959.
The Moon likely formed after a Mars-sized object collided with early Earth.
Much of the Moon's early global magma ocean had crystallized within about 100 million years.
The Moon has a core, mantle, and crust.
The Moon's crust is thicker on the far side than on the near side.
The dark lunar plains called maria are ancient impact basins filled by lava.
The light regions on the Moon are called highlands.
The Moon's powdery surface layer is called lunar regolith.
Tycho, a prominent lunar crater, is more than 85 kilometers wide.
Lunar craters form when asteroids, meteoroids, or comets strike the surface.
Some material blasted out by lunar impacts can reach orbit; lunar meteorites have been found on Earth.
The largest impact craters are relatively shallow compared with their diameter.
The Moon is about one-third Earth's width.
The Moon slowly moves about an inch farther from Earth each year.
The Moon can reach about 127°C in sunlight and about -173°C in darkness.
NASA's SOFIA observatory confirmed water molecules on the sunlit Moon in 2020.

mountain_weather.text: Glaciers are moving masses of ice that can carve and sculpt mountain landscapes.
Glaciers can carve steep-walled, flat-bottomed U-shaped valleys.
A fjord is one kind of valley that glaciers can carve.
Glaciers can leave hanging valleys where smaller ice streams met larger glaciers.
A horn is a sharp peak carved by glaciers on three or more sides.
An arête is a sharp ridge shaped by glaciers eroding both sides.
Glaciers grow when winter snow accumulation exceeds summer melting.
A glacier retreats when melting outpaces snowfall; retreat does not mean it flows uphill.
Glacier ice can erode rock by abrasion and by plucking chunks from bedrock.
Glaciers transport rocks and sediment as they flow.
Mountains are shaped over time by water, wind, ice, and gravity.
Moving tectonic plates help build mountains and volcanoes.
Volcanoes can build mountains by adding erupted material.
Mauna Kea is the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from its underwater base.
Water running downhill can carry sediment from mountain slopes into streams.
Young, tall mountains often have steeper slopes than older, lower ranges.
Mount Rainier is encircled by 25 glaciers, according to the National Park Service.
Mount Rainier's glaciers have carved valleys and moved rock over thousands of years.
A mass of ice can flow under its own weight once it is large enough to behave as a glacier.
Many glaciers cover at least 0.1 square kilometer, though some smaller active glaciers are exceptions.
A cirque is a steep-walled, bowl-shaped hollow carved high on a mountain by ice.
Ridges of rock deposited along a glacier's edge are called moraines.
The Continental Divide follows the crest of the Lewis Range in Glacier National Park.
Glacier National Park contains parts of the Livingston and Lewis mountain ranges.
Mountains in Glacier National Park record more than a billion years of geological change.
Snow crystals bond together as layers of snow compress into glacial ice.
Snowflakes begin when a cold water droplet freezes onto a tiny particle in the air.
Snow crystals have six-sided symmetry because of how water molecules arrange in ice.
Temperature and humidity help determine the shape of a growing snow crystal.
Each snowflake follows a different path through changing air, helping make its shape unique.

forest.text: Green plants use photosynthesis to turn sunlight into stored energy.
Photosynthesis produces sugars, oxygen, and water that support other life.
A forest canopy is the upper layer made by treetops reaching toward the sky.
Forests provide shelter and food for many kinds of plants and animals.
In Katahdin Woods and Waters, forests cover about 90 percent of the monument.
An animal's habitat provides the food, shelter, space, and water it needs.
Black bears can climb trees.
Black bears may have black, brown, blond, or cinnamon-colored fur.
Grizzly bears eat both plants and animals, so they are omnivores.
Grizzly bears can run up to about 45 miles per hour.
Grizzly bears rub trees, and the hair left behind can help scientists study them.
Pine martens can be spotted surveying forest branches.
At Minute Man, squirrels can leap up to 10 feet from tree to tree.
Squirrels sometimes forget where they buried nuts, giving some seeds a chance to grow.
Bats can be prey for forest predators such as owls, foxes, and snakes.
A forest ecosystem includes living organisms and nonliving parts of their habitat.
Food webs link many food chains because animals can have more than one food source.
The Sun supplies energy that fuels food webs.
Plants are producers because they can make food using photosynthesis.
Herbivores such as rabbits eat plants directly and are primary consumers.
Animals may use different forest layers, from the canopy down to underground burrows.
The way habitat features connect across land affects habitat quality for wildlife.
Gray jays often rest and nest near the tops of evergreen trees.
Mount Rainier National Park has recorded 182 bird species.
Leaves are a site where plants make food through photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis uses sunlight, carbon dioxide from air, and water from soil to make plant food.
A sapling is a young tree with a slender trunk.
Glucose is a sugar plants make during photosynthesis and use as an energy source.
Mushrooms and fungi are important parts of park ecosystems, with thousands of species in national parks.
More than 75 percent of Earth's flowering plants depend on pollinators, including bees.

technology.text: A telegraph sent electrical signals over wires to communicate across distance.
Samuel Morse sent a historic telegraph message between Washington and Baltimore in 1844.
Morse Code uses short and long signals to represent letters and numbers.
Morse Code gave frequently used letters shorter codes to make signaling efficient.
Before electrical telegraphs, messages could travel by horse or by visual signals such as smoke.
Alexander Graham Bell's telephone converted sound vibrations into electrical signals and back into sound.
Bell's successful telephone test with Thomas Watson took place in 1876.
Several inventors, including Bell and Elisha Gray, worked on early telephone ideas.
Thomas Edison tested hundreds of materials while developing a practical lamp filament.
Edison's 1879 lamp used a carbon filament inside a glass bulb.
An electric lamp needs a filament that glows without burning or breaking too quickly.
Edison and his team also developed generators, cables, and meters for an electric lighting system.
Beulah Louise Henry received 49 patents between 1912 and 1962.
Beulah Henry designed a vacuum ice-cream freezer that reduced the work of cranking.
John Fitch's early steamboat design used steam-powered oars before he switched to paddlewheels.
Steam engines move pistons using steam from boiling water.
A touch screen can detect a finger by sensing a change in an electrical current.
The Library of Congress describes Velcro as an example of design inspired by nature.
Edison received U.S. patent 90,646 for an electric vote recorder on June 1, 1869; it was never used.
Edison developed a quadruplex telegraph in 1874 that could send four messages over one wire at once.
Edison filed his phonograph patent in 1877; it was granted on February 19, 1878.
Edison worked on motion pictures starting in the late 1880s.
Edison's laboratory team helped test and improve inventions; invention is often collaborative.
The Library of Congress notes that inventions often build on earlier technologies and ideas.
Morse's notebooks document experiments and plans for the telegraph.
Bell's notebooks record his telephone plans and experiments.
The first transatlantic telegraph cable was laid in 1858, but it soon failed.
A practical light bulb required a vacuum inside the glass envelope to protect its filament.
Edison's carbon filament had high electrical resistance, helping heat build up in the filament.
The telephone made real-time voice communication possible over a distance.

water_cycle.text: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water through Earth and its atmosphere.
Water naturally exists as solid ice, liquid water, and water vapor.
Evaporation changes liquid water into water vapor.
Water can evaporate from oceans, lakes, rain, and even small puddles.
Plants release water vapor from their leaves in a process called transpiration.
Condensation turns water vapor into liquid droplets and can form clouds or dew.
Precipitation returns water from clouds to Earth as rain, snow, or other forms.
Runoff is water that flows over land and can feed streams, rivers, and lakes.
Infiltration happens when water on the ground moves into soil.
Water that moves deeper through soil can replenish groundwater.
Snow or ice can change directly into water vapor through sublimation.
Water vapor can change directly into ice by deposition, forming frost.
Clouds moving across the sky show water being transported through the atmosphere.
The Sun supplies energy that helps water evaporate.
Condensation releases heat into the surrounding environment.
Precipitation includes rain, hail, snow, and sleet.
Precipitation is the primary way fresh water reaches Earth's surface.
When rain exceeds what soil can absorb, extra water can become runoff.
Evaporation can leave salts and impurities behind in a lake with no outlet.
Water stored in glaciers can melt and move into oceans and other liquid-water stores.
Some water vapor comes back to the ground as rain; some can fall as snow.
Water absorbed by plant roots can later return to the air through transpiration.
Air cooling can cause water vapor to condense into droplets.
Tiny cloud droplets can combine and grow before falling as precipitation.
Ice crystals can grow in cold clouds and later fall as snow or ice pellets.
If cloud air and the air all the way to the ground are freezing, precipitation can reach us as snow.
Warm air can hold more water vapor before it becomes saturated and condenses.
Longer gaps between rain can happen even as warmer air contributes to heavier rainfall.
Water moves between oceans, clouds, lakes, vegetation, snowpack, and glaciers.
Rain that flows over land can carry water from mountains into rivers.
